To fix it, we refactored our state machine to prioritize optimistic UI updates. Now, the client assumes success immediately after the gateway callback, while a silent database query handles any delays in the background. Latency dropped to almost zero.

It made me realize how much of good UX is just hiding backend latency from the user.

Waiting for a backend response to update a cart UI feels incredibly outdated.

When you add an item to your cart on Amazon, the UI updates instantly. There is no spinner, no lag, and no waiting for a server confirmation.

I wanted that exact same zero-latency feel for STRAYED.

To get there, I implemented optimistic client-side updates in our frontend. When a user clicks 'Add to Cart', we immediately update the local React State to reflect the new item, while the actual API request to our MedusaJS backend runs silently in the background.

If the server request fails for some rare reason, we gracefully roll back the UI state and show a quick notification. But 99% of the time, the user experiences an instant, snappy transition.

It is a small detail, but these micro-interactions are what separate clean, premium products from clunky web pages.

Our database logs showed a recurring spike in query latency every Tuesday at midnight. I spent three nights trying to find a misconfigured cron job or a heavy API call that might be causing the database to choke. It felt like a ghost in the machine because the server load appeared normal on all monitoring dashboards.

It turned out that our automated backup script on the Oracle VPS was locking the PostgreSQL table indices during a full snapshot. Because the database was essentially freezing to ensure consistency, any incoming customer requests during those ten minutes would queue up and cause a massive bottleneck. The fix was surprisingly simple once I realized it was an infrastructure issue rather than an application code bug.

I shifted the backup window to a lower-traffic period and implemented a read-only replica for non-critical dashboard queries. It freed up our primary instance to handle store transactions without being interrupted by maintenance tasks. This experience taught me that sometimes your application performance issues have absolutely nothing to do with your code and everything to do with server-level configuration.

I spent three days trying to fix a ghost database connection timeout. 

Every time our traffic spiked past a few hundred concurrent users, our database connection pool would just stop responding. My initial instinct was to blame the VPS provider and look for a bigger server instance to throw at the problem. 

It turned out to be a classic connection leak in our Node.js middleware. I was opening a new database client for every single incoming request but failing to release it back to the pool once the operation finished. The server was effectively hitting a dead end because the pool was full of abandoned connections. 

I swapped the manual connection management for a proper persistent pool configuration and wrapped the queries in a try-finally block. The resource consumption dropped by sixty percent instantly, and the site stopped hanging under load. 

We often look for complex infrastructure solutions when the bottleneck is usually a simple case of improper resource handling in our own code.
